subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the area of the region bounded by the parabolas y² = 4x and x² = 4y.

mark_split.label: Solve for the points of intersection
Identify the upper and lower curves

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book printed p.71 — SAQ chapter 10 'Definite Integrals', sub-heading 'AREAS', answer 90, the second of the three area questions on this page. Printed appearance: TS 17. Chapter star rank ★★★ applies. The book draws a small sketch of the two parabolas with the enclosed lens-shaped region hatched and labelled A, next to the equations — reproduced here as a figure because the region is the intersection of two curves and the picture is what makes 'upper curve' and 'lower curve' legible. No margin mark tags are printed, so the 1+1+2 split is OURS, patterned on the shape of the neighbouring area answer 89 (same three-stage pattern) on this same page. Boundary reading: printed p.67 and printed p.72 confirm the chapter span. No two-book union check and no board back-test were possible for Maths-2B (no second-year TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand; the book's five Guess Papers pp.118-127 stand in for the back-test).

insider_note: Both parabolas pass through the origin, so x = 0 is always one intersection — the real work is finding the second one, x = 4, by eliminating y between the two equations.

steps.label: Solve for the points of intersection
steps.margin_note: One mark. Eliminate y first, then factor out x rather than dividing.
steps.memory_tip: Both parabolas pass through the origin, so x = 0 is always one root — look for the second root separately.
steps.why: Substituting y from the second equation into the first eliminates y, leaving a single equation in x whose two roots (0 and 4) are the x-coordinates of the two points where the parabolas cross.
common_mistakes: Dividing by x instead of factoring, which loses the root x = 0.
An arithmetic slip in x⁴ = 64x, e.g. reaching x³ = 16 instead of x³ = 64.

steps.label: Identify the upper and lower curves
steps.margin_note: One more mark. The picture makes it obvious which curve bounds the region from above.
steps.memory_tip: y² = 4x opens sideways and lies on top of the region; x² = 4y opens upward and lies underneath.
steps.why: y² = 4x is a sideways-opening parabola whose upper branch y = 2√x lies above the region, while x² = 4y is an upward-opening parabola whose branch y = x²/4 lies below it — the picture makes this ordering immediate, which is what the integral setup depends on.
common_mistakes: Confusing which parabola is which — y² = 4x opens along the x-axis, x² = 4y opens along the y-axis.
Setting up the integral with the two curves swapped, which gives a negative area.

steps.label: Integrate and evaluate
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Write y = 2√x as the upper curve and y = x²/4 as the lower curve before integrating.
steps.memory_tip: y² = 4x gives y = 2√x (upper); x² = 4y gives y = x²/4 (lower) — always upper minus lower.
steps.why: Integrating the upper curve minus the lower curve from x = 0 to x = 4 (the two intersection points) and substituting the limits (the lower limit contributes 0) gives 32/3 − 16/3, a clean fraction.
common_mistakes: Losing the coefficient 2 in front of (2/3)x^(3/2) while combining terms.
